prompt.context: You have been relatively successful in your post-MBA career and are considering quitting to move to a holiday destination in Southeast Asia and open a resort there.
prompt.question: Should you open a resort, and if so, where should you open it?

clarifying_info.q: How many staff would I employ?
clarifying_info.a: You plan to employ 5 people in your resort.

clarifying_info.q: Would I leave my current job?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, you are considering leaving your current position to build this resort full time.
At a minimum, you want the resort to generate as much cash flow as you made in your last job.

clarifying_info.q: What salary should I use for my current job?
clarifying_info.a: It is up to you to apply your own salary and conditions of your current job.

clarifying_info.q: Are city destinations also on the table?
clarifying_info.a: No, you are only considering resort destinations. You are tired of the bustle of city life.

exhibits.title: Southeast Asia Resort Destination Comparison
exhibits.shows: A table comparing four candidate resort destinations — Bali, Penang, Boracay, and Phuket — across seven metrics.

framework: Qualitative factors: assess personal readiness, cultural fit, lifestyle change, type of resort and activities to host
Status quo baseline: quantify current job cash flow as the minimum hurdle rate for the resort
Revenue analysis: estimate total tourist market per destination (international + domestic tourists, receipts, length of stay)
Market share estimate: assume mean market share across all resorts in the chosen destination
Cost structure: wages (20% of operating costs), land, and PPE
Profitability comparison: compare projected resort cash flow vs current salary
Location selection: rank destinations on market size, growth rate, and competitive intensity

questions.prompt: Walk through the qualitative factors you would consider before deciding to open a resort.
questions.guidance: Strong answers cover: personal/cultural readiness (culture shock, language, local knowledge), type of resort and activities that match personal strengths, lifestyle change from city to resort environment, long-term career and life satisfaction. The candidate should treat this as a genuine personal decision, not just a financial one.

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 1, which destination would you prioritise and why?
questions.guidance: Key insights: Phuket has the largest market (39M international arrivals, USD 65.2B tourist receipts) but also the most resorts (200) and slowest GDP growth (2%). Boracay has the smallest market (7M arrivals, USD 9.7B receipts) but the fewest resorts (20) and highest GDP growth (7%) — least competitive, fastest-growing. Penang has the highest GDP/capita (USD 33,000). A strong candidate notes the trade-off between market size and saturation and uses growth rates to assess future attractiveness.

questions.prompt: Estimate the annual revenue per resort in Phuket (or your chosen destination).
questions.guidance: The candidate should build up from tourist receipts per visitor per day, then scale to a single resort assuming a mean market share. Key assumptions to surface: share of tourist receipts spent on accommodation, number of rooms, persons per room, and occupancy rate.

math.setup: Using Phuket: USD 65.2B total tourist receipts, 39M international visitors, average 7-day country stay, average 4-day resort stay. Assume 50% of receipts on accommodation, 100 rooms per resort, 2 persons per room, 80% occupancy. 200 resorts in Phuket implies mean market share = 1/200.
steps: Revenue per visitor per day: USD 65.2B * 50% / 39M visitors / 7 days ≈ USD 115 per person per day
Annual resort revenue (100 rooms, 2 pax/room, 80% occupancy, 365 days): USD 115 * 100 * 2 * 365 * 0.80 ≈ USD 6.6M
Mean market share per resort: USD 6.6M (each resort assumed identical at mean; total market = 200 * USD 6.6M = USD 1.32B)
math.answer: Approximately USD 6.6M revenue per resort per year in Phuket at mean market share.

questions.prompt: Now estimate the cost structure and check whether this exceeds your current salary.
questions.guidance: Wages are 20% of total operating costs. With 5 employees, the candidate should estimate reasonable wages for Southeast Asia (or use their own assumed salary level). Total operating costs = wages / 20%. The candidate must then compare net cash flow (revenue minus costs) to their assumed current salary. A strong candidate explicitly states the hurdle rate and whether the resort clears it.

math.setup: Wages = 5 employees * assumed average local wage (candidate to specify). Wages = 20% of total operating costs, so total operating costs = wages / 0.20. Net cash flow = revenue - total operating costs.
steps: Net cash flow = USD 6.6M - USD 500,000 = USD 6.1M
Compare USD 6.1M to assumed post-MBA salary (e.g., USD 150,000–300,000) — resort far exceeds hurdle if Phuket figures hold
math.answer: Resort cash flow likely exceeds a typical post-MBA salary if the market-share and revenue assumptions hold, but the candidate should sanity-check by applying their own salary.

recommendation: The resort venture can make financial sense — estimated resort revenue at mean market share in Phuket (~USD 6.6M/year) greatly exceeds a typical post-MBA salary, providing strong upside if costs are controlled.

Boracay is the most attractive destination on a risk-adjusted basis: lowest competition (20 resorts), fastest GDP growth (7%), and a smaller but rapidly expanding market — easier to capture above-mean market share as an early entrant.
Phuket offers the largest absolute market but is the most saturated (200 resorts, 2% growth), making it harder to differentiate and capture share.
risks: Execution risk: building and operating a resort is operationally complex, especially in an unfamiliar country (regulation, permits, construction quality).
Currency and macro risk: revenues in local currency or USD but cost of living and capital requirements may shift.
Overestimated market share: mean market share assumes all resorts are equal; a new entrant may underperform initially.
Personal risk: leaving a stable post-MBA career is irreversible in the short term; lifestyle change may not suit everyone.
Market saturation could worsen in high-growth destinations as other investors respond to the same growth signals.
next_steps: Visit shortlisted destinations (Boracay and Phuket) to conduct on-the-ground due diligence on land costs, regulatory environment, and competitive landscape.
Model a detailed P&L with local wage data, land/construction costs, and financing costs.
Assess personal qualitative fit: language, culture, lifestyle preferences.
Identify a local partner or operator to reduce execution risk.
Stress-test the revenue model under lower occupancy (e.g., 60%) and lower market share scenarios.
